Plot scores across training sizes

learning_curve fits a fresh model with different training-set sizes in each cross-validation split. Plot the mean training and validation accuracy at each size. Shuffling the subset selection here suits the independent records in this example. Choose a splitter that matches time ordering or grouped data when those structures exist.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, learning_curve
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
sizes, train, valid = learning_curve(
    model, X, y, train_sizes=[0.15, 0.35, 0.60, 1.0], cv=cv,
    scoring="accuracy", shuffle=True, random_state=42,
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(layout="constrained")
ax.plot(sizes, train.mean(axis=1), "o-", label="Training")
ax.plot(sizes, valid.mean(axis=1), "s--", label="Validation")
ax.set(xlabel="Training examples per fold", ylabel="Mean accuracy")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

Interpret the gap and the score levels

A persistent gap with a high training score can suggest overfitting. Two similarly low curves can suggest underfitting or limited predictive features. Compare against a baseline and check variation across folds. Keep a separate test set for the final evaluation when choosing models based on validation results.
